compoundNote: Lemon balm (Melissa officinalis) trials use very different preparations: standardised extracts and dried leaf at single doses of 300 to 1600 mg (2002 to 2004 crossover studies), a branded phospholipid-carrier aqueous extract (Relissa, Indena; 400 mg/day) in the recent sleep trials, rosmarinic-acid-standardised extract (500 mg rosmarinic acid/day) in cognition trials in older adults, gram-level capsule doses in Iranian clinical populations, and combinations with valerian, Nepeta, fennel, theanine or saffron. Results from one preparation do not transfer to another; the Performance Lab Sleep label gives 200 mg per serving of lemon balm extract with the extract type and standardisation not stated, so only the dose and the genus are comparable. Many sleep trials are small, short, combination-based or run by the product maker; null results (PMIDs 38580720, 37131158 for sleep, 36502333 for cognition) are listed alongside the positives. verdicts.claim: Sleep quality in adults with poor sleep or emotional distress (phospholipid-carrier lemon balm extract, 400 mg/day)
verdicts.reason: Two placebo-controlled trials of the same branded phospholipid extract report better sleep: a 30-person crossover (400 mg/day, 2 weeks, ISI -2.9 points, p=0.003) and a 100-person parallel trial (400 mg/day, 3 weeks, PSQI group x time p<0.001, but with significantly worse baseline PSQI in the active group). An open-label dose comparison (n=32) adds uncontrolled support, with a smaller PSQI change at 200 mg (-15%) than at 400 mg (-30%). All three concern one product (Relissa, Indena) with manufacturer-linked authors or trademarks, follow-up is 2 to 3 weeks, and no independent replication exists.

verdicts.claim: Sleep in clinical or herbal-combination settings (menopause, insomnia clinics, cardiac patients, diabetes)
verdicts.reason: Small trials, mostly from Iran and mostly combinations: lemon balm + Nepeta for insomnia (ISI, PSQI better, 4 weeks), valerian/lemon balm in menopausal women (PSQI better), 3 g/day lemon balm in angina patients (PSQI better, 8 weeks). A 700 mg/day lemon balm extract in type 2 diabetes had no effect on PSQI, and a four-herb formula with theanine, valerian and saffron was null on actigraphy and PSQI (6 weeks). Lemon balm cannot be isolated from the combinations, doses are often not stated, and some abstracts lack sample size or funding detail.

verdicts.claim: Acute calmness / stress and anxiety in healthy adults
verdicts.reason: Single-dose crossover trials of 18 to 24 people found more self-rated calmness at 600 mg (2004), at the lowest dose early on (2002) and at 1600 mg of dried leaf (2003) but with reduced alertness, worse memory factors or slower task speed at some doses, and inconsistent dose-response. A 106-person trial of 300 mg missed its primary calmness endpoint but showed better calmness recovery and hard-task performance at 5 h. Food-matrix studies (sponsor-involved) report mood gains with behavioural costs. All effects are acute and laboratory-based; no controlled multi-week trial in healthy adults with anxiety as the primary outcome was found.

verdicts.claim: Anxiety and depressive symptoms in symptomatic or clinical populations
verdicts.reason: The only meta-analysis located (published 2021) reports SMD -0.98 for anxiety and -0.47 for depression with 'high heterogeneity' and few trials; individual trials in type 2 diabetes (700 mg/day, 12 weeks: depression p<0.001, anxiety p=0.04) and angina patients (3 g/day, 8 weeks) are positive but small. The meta-analysis authors warn the results need caution; the trial count and risk-of-bias detail were not in the abstract.

Acute trials show a mix of gains and losses: accuracy of attention up but memory factors down (2002, 300-900 mg), memory up at 1600 mg but slower tasks at lower doses (2003), better hardest-task executive function at 5 h after 300 mg (2026). No chronic-dosing cognition RCT in healthy adults was found. Effects depend on preparation and dose and do not form a consistent pattern.

verdicts.claim: Cognition in older adults, MCI and Alzheimer's disease
verdicts.reason: The largest and longest trial (n=323, 500 mg rosmarinic acid/day for 96 weeks) was null on its primary cognitive endpoint, with only a post hoc subgroup signal. A small 24-week trial in mild AD (n=23) was null on cognition but improved neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPI-Q). A 2003 Iranian trial (n=42, 4 months) was positive on ADAS-cog. Not a healthy-adult nootropic effect; relevant to the product only as background.

verdicts.claim: Lemon balm as one ingredient in a multi-ingredient sleep formula
verdicts.reason: The single placebo-controlled trial found that included lemon balm with L-theanine, valerian and saffron (n=64, 6 weeks) was null on actigraphy and PSQI. Positive combination trials exist (with Nepeta or valerian) but not with magnesium, tryptophan or cherry. No trial combining lemon balm with tart cherry was found.

doseAssessment.trialRange: Sleep trials with positive results: 400 mg/day of a phospholipid-carrier aqueous extract (Relissa, standardised to 17-23% hydroxycinnamic acid derivatives), taken as 2 x 200 mg tablets, for 2 to 3 weeks (PMIDs 39683592, 37927585); 200 vs 400 mg/day in an open-label study without placebo (PMID 41777239: PSQI -15% vs -30%); 1000 mg dry powder + 400 mg Nepeta extract nightly for 4 weeks (PMID 29741926); 3 g/day capsules for 8 weeks in angina (PMID 29908682). Null or no-effect on sleep: 700 mg/day hydroalcoholic extract for 12 weeks (PMID 37131158); a theanine + lemon balm + valerian + saffron formula for 6 weeks (PMID 38580720, doses not stated). Stress/mood/cognition: single doses of 300, 600, 900 mg (standardised extract), 600, 1000, 1600 mg (dried leaf), 1.8 g extract (2% rosmarinic acid) in a drink, 0.3 or 0.6 g in yoghurt, 300 mg (Zensera); older adults 500 mg rosmarinic acid/day for 24 to 96 weeks.
doseAssessment.suggestedText: Performance Lab Sleep gives 200 mg of lemon balm extract per 2-capsule serving, with the extract type and standardisation not stated on the label. That is BELOW every stated dose with a positive result in the sleep trials above (400 mg/day of a standardised phospholipid extract; 1 g to 3 g/day of other preparations) and below the lowest single dose tested in the stress and cognition crossover trials (300 mg). It matches only the 200 mg arm of an uncontrolled open-label study, where the PSQI change was half that at 400 mg (-15% vs -30%, PMID 41777239). Because the product's extract ratio, rosmarinic acid content and carrier are unknown, we cannot say how much active material 200 mg delivers compared with the branded phospholipid extract (designed for higher bioavailability) or with the dried leaf and 2%-rosmarinic-acid extracts used in other trials; equivalence is not established. No trial tested lemon balm at 200 mg per day taken together with magnesium, tryptophan and tart cherry.

safetySignals.signal: Dose-dependent daytime effects in healthy young adults: self-rated alertness was significantly reduced at all time points after the highest dose (900 mg), and secondary- and working-memory factors were reduced at some times and doses. A similar alertness decrease came with 600 mg in the stress study (PMID 15272110). Relevant to evening use only for next-day grogginess; not measured.
safetySignals.title: Modulation of mood and cognitive performance following acute administration of Melissa officinalis (lemon balm)

safetySignals.signal: Lemon balm + valerian combination: the 1800 mg dose increased anxiety at one test session and all doses (600-1800 mg) impaired Stroop task performance; the 600 mg dose reduced stress-related anxiety. A reminder that a higher dose is not better.
safetySignals.title: Anxiolytic effects of a combination of Melissa officinalis and Valeriana officinalis during laboratory induced stress

safetySignals.signal: Longest human exposure found: 500 mg rosmarinic acid/day extract for 96 weeks in 323 older adults with subjective or mild cognitive impairment - no differences in vital signs, physical and neurological measures or hippocampal volume vs placebo (adverse-event table not read).
safetySignals.title: Effects of Melissa officinalis Extract Containing Rosmarinic Acid on Cognition in Older Adults Without Dementia: A Randomized Controlled Trial

safetySignals.signal: 500 mg rosmarinic acid/day for 24 weeks in 23 patients with mild AD dementia: no serious adverse events and no vital-sign or exam differences vs placebo. Very small sample.
safetySignals.title: Safety and efficacy of Melissa officinalis extract containing rosmarinic acid in the prevention of Alzheimer's disease progression

safetySignals.signal: Single 500 mg rosmarinic acid dose in 11 healthy volunteers: no adverse events, no change in liver, kidney or blood-cell parameters; food raised exposure and delayed absorption.
safetySignals.title: Pharmacokinetics, Safety and Tolerability of Melissa officinalis Extract which Contained Rosmarinic Acid in Healthy Individuals: A Randomized Controlled Trial

safetySignals.signal: Animal data only, not human: 90-day rat study of an aqueous lemon balm extract found no test-substance-related adverse effects (NOAEL at least 3046 mg/kg/day in males and 3721 in females, the highest doses tested). The authors are employees of the extract's manufacturer (Givaudan).
safetySignals.title: Toxicological safety evaluation of an aqueous lemon balm (Melissa officinalis) extract

gaps: The strongest sleep evidence is for one branded phospholipid extract (Relissa, Indena): a 30-person crossover and a 100-person parallel trial plus an uncontrolled open-label study, all 2 to 3 weeks, all with manufacturer-linked authors or trademark disclosure. No independent replication, and no trial of an unstandardised or unspecified lemon balm extract at 200 mg/day for sleep was found.

Performance Lab Sleep does not state the extract type or standardisation, so the 200 mg per serving cannot be placed against any trialled preparation. Rosmarinic acid content, extract ratio and carrier are unknown (needs the product's certificate of analysis).

Many sleep trials use lemon balm combined with valerian or Nepeta (PMIDs 29741926, 30591886, 24199972) or a menopause product whose registry title names other plants (PMID 33465795); lemon balm's separate contribution is not testable from these.
Several abstracts omit sample size, dose, duration or funding (PMIDs 29741926, 24199972, 25360512, 34449930, 22207903); these were not resolved because the full texts are paywalled or were not read.

No chronic-dosing cognition RCT in healthy adults was found; the acute trials (2002 to 2004, 18 to 24 volunteers) show gains and losses depending on dose, and the largest 96-week trial in people with subjective or mild cognitive impairment (PMID 36502333) was null on its primary endpoint.

The only anxiety/depression meta-analysis located (PMID 34449930, 2021) reports high heterogeneity and does not give the number of trials or risk-of-bias in its abstract; no sleep-specific meta-analysis of lemon balm was found (a 2025 narrative review, PMID 41226605, and an industry-funded 2024 review, PMID 39458539, were located but are not pooled analyses).

No human data on interactions of lemon balm with sedatives, sleep medication, alcohol, thyroid medication or in pregnancy and breastfeeding was read: a thyroid-related PubMed hit (PMID 14759065, an in vitro assay) and case reports were found but not read, so no safety conclusion is drawn about them. Absence of evidence is not evidence of safety.
No trial combined lemon balm, tart cherry, magnesium and L-tryptophan, so the interaction of the full Performance Lab Sleep formula is untested here.
